steps.explanationAfterStep: The bromonium ion: bromine bridges both carbons and carries the positive charge. No open carbocation forms, so nothing rearranges, and the bridge blocks one face of the ring.
Bromide attacks from the face opposite the bridge, as in SN2. The bromines end up trans: anti addition. (Stereochemistry is shown here, not checked.)

title: Bromination of cyclohexene
subtitle: A bromonium ion, opened from the back
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 20

reactants.caption: cyclohexene + bromine
hintTiers: Br₂ has no charge, but the electron-rich π bond polarises it. Which part is the electrophile?
The π bond attacks the near bromine and the Br–Br bond breaks onto the far one. At the same time a lone pair on the near bromine bonds to the other alkene carbon. Three arrows.
Arrow 1: from the C=C π bond to the near bromine, forming one C–Br bond. Arrow 2: from a lone pair of that bromine to the other alkene carbon. Arrow 3: from the Br–Br bond onto the far bromine.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Bromine adds to cyclohexene. Draw the first step: it makes a three-membered ring.

misconceptions.arrowPattern: π C1-C2 -> σ C1-Br7;σ Br7-Br8 -> lp Br7
misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The Br–Br electrons go to the far bromine, which leaves as bromide. The near bromine, the one the π bond attacks, keeps its lone pairs and uses one to bond to the second carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: That would give an open carbocation. With bromine, a lone pair of the attached bromine bonds to the cationic carbon at the same time: add that arrow.
Right start. Bromine now has two bonds: break the Br–Br bond, and let the attached bromine close a ring to the other carbon.

bromonium-ion.caption: the bromonium ion + bromide
hintTiers: This is like an SN2 reaction. What is the nucleophile, and what is the leaving group?
Bromide attacks one ring carbon from the face opposite the bromonium bromine, and that C–Br bond breaks onto the positive bromine. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: from a bromide lone pair to one carbon of the three-membered ring. Arrow 2: from that carbon's bond to the ring bromine onto the ring bromine.
bromonium-ion.learnerPrompt: Bromide opens the bromonium ion. Draw it.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Attack at bromine would just give back Br₂ and the alkene. Bromide attacks a carbon of the ring.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right target. That carbon now has five bonds: break its bond to the ring bromine.

mechanismSummary: The alkene π bond attacks one bromine as the Br–Br bond breaks, and a lone pair of that bromine bonds to the other alkene carbon: a three-membered bromonium ion. Bromide opens it from the opposite face, like an SN2 reaction, so the two bromines end up on opposite faces: trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane (anti addition).
